title: Wind effect on a plane
text:
One plane does a round trip from A to B in a straight line. Compare the time of the round trip if there is no wind and if there is a constant wind.






Tip💡 Hint





You can either use intuition about the effect of the wind during the trip A-B and during the trip B-A or you can use basic physics by introducing the speed of the plane and the speed of the wind.









Tip💡 Solution





Let’s assume a constant wind in the direction A towards B.
For the intuition part, the wind will make the plane go faster on the trip A-B but slower on the trip B-A. Thus, the trip A-B will take less time than the trip B-A and the advantage of being in the same direction as the wind will weight less than the disadvantage of facing the wind. Therefore, the round trip will take more time if there is wind.
Mathematically, let \(s\) be the speed of the plane without wind, \(w\) be the speed of the wind and \(d\) the distance AB. Since time is additive, if no wind we have \(t_{\text{no wind}}=t_{AB} + t_{BA} = \frac{d}{s} + \frac{d}{s} = \frac{2d}{s}.\) Now, in there is wind in the direction A to B, then the speed on the trip A-B will be \(s+w\) and the speed on the trip B-A will be \(s-w\). Thus, we have \(t_{\text{wind}}=t_{AB} + t_{BA} = \frac{d}{s+w} + \frac{d}{s-w} = \frac{2ds}{s^2-w^2} = \frac{2d}{s-w^2/s}.\) Since \(w^2/s>0\), we have \(\boxed{t_{\text{wind}} > t_{\text{no wind}}.}\)

title: Average of three integers
text:
Question
We randomly select 3 distinct integers from \(\{1,2,\dots,30\}\). What is the probability that one of the numbers is the average of the other two?






Tip💡 Solution





Total number of ways to choose 3 distinct integers from \(\{1,\dots,30\}\) is
\(\binom{30}{3} = 4060\).


Step 1: Characterising valid triples
We want triples \(\{a,b,c\}\) such that one number is the average of the other two.
If we order them as \(a < b < c\), this condition becomes:
\(b = \frac{a+c}{2}\)
So \((a,b,c)\) must form an arithmetic progression of length 3: \(a, a+d, a+2d\).



Step 2: Counting valid triples
We need:
\(a + 2d \le 30\)
So for each \(d \ge 1\), the number of choices for \(a\) is:
\(30 - 2d\)
The maximum possible \(d\) is \(14\).
Hence the number of valid triples is:
\(\sum_{d=1}^{14} (30 - 2d)\)
Compute:
\(\sum_{d=1}^{14} 30 = 420\)
\(\sum_{d=1}^{14} 2d = 2 \cdot \frac{14 \cdot 15}{2} = 210\)
So total favorable triples:
\(420 - 210 = 210\)



Step 3: Probability
\(\frac{210}{4060} = \frac{21}{406} = \frac{3}{58}\)



Final answer
\(\boxed{\frac{3}{58}}\)

title: Russian bullet cylinder
text:
A criminal but two bullets in a row in a six bullet cylinder. He shuffles it and shot once, nothing happens. Is it better for you to reshuffle or not ?






Tip💡 Solution





Imagine that the bullets are in slot 1 and 2 and that the cylinder goes increasingly, the cycle is therefore (1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6).

If you reshuffle, every slot is equally plausible and \(\mathbb{P}(\text{death | shuffle)} = 1/3\).
If you don’t reshuffle, since the first shot was blank, you know that you are not in slots 1 nor 2. Among the 4 slots left, only the slot 6 would lead to a bullet at the next shot. Therefore, \(\mathbb{P}(\text{death | no shuffle)} = 1/4.\)

Thus, it is better to not reshuffle.

title: Circular Table
text:
Question : Probability that a 3-legged circular table can stand
Suppose a circular table has 3 legs placed uniformly at random on the circumference of the tabletop. What is the probability that the table can stand?






Tip💡 Solution





The table stands if and only if the center of the circle lies inside the triangle formed by the three legs.
For three points chosen uniformly at random on a circle, the center lies inside the triangle exactly when the three points are not all contained in a semicircle.
A classical result states that for \(n\) random points on a circle, the probability that they all lie in some semicircle is \(\frac{n}{2^{n-1}}\) (Take the semicircle starting at each point the other ones have prob 1/2 to be clockwise and sum over the points to have the semicircle starting at the left most point).
For \(n=3\), this gives \(\frac{3}{2^2}=\frac34.\) Therefore, the probability that the points are not all contained in a semicircle is \(1-\frac34=\frac14.\) Hence, \(\boxed{\frac14}.\)

title: Expected value of a dice game
text:
Question
We roll 3 fair six-sided dice. If all three numbers are the same, we win $20. If exactly two numbers are the same, we win $10. If all three numbers are different, we lose $2. What is the expected return per roll?






Tip💡 Solution





Total number of outcomes when rolling 3 dice is
\(6^3 = 216\)


Step 1: Compute probabilities

Case 1: All three the same
There are 6 outcomes: \((1,1,1)\) to \((6,6,6)\)
Probability:
\(\frac{6}{216} = \frac{1}{36}\)



Case 2: Exactly two the same
Choose the repeated number: \(6\) ways
Choose the different number: \(5\) ways
Choose position of different die: \(3\) ways
Total:
\(6 \cdot 5 \cdot 3 = 90\)
Probability:
\(\frac{90}{216} = \frac{5}{12}\)



Case 3: All different
Remaining outcomes:
\(216 - 6 - 90 = 120\)
Probability:
\(\frac{120}{216} = \frac{5}{9}\)




Step 2: Expected value
Expected return is
\(E = 20 \cdot \frac{1}{36} + 10 \cdot \frac{5}{12} - 2 \cdot \frac{5}{9}\)
Compute each term:
\(20 \cdot \frac{1}{36} = \frac{5}{9}\)
\(10 \cdot \frac{5}{12} = \frac{25}{6}\)
\(-2 \cdot \frac{5}{9} = -\frac{10}{9}\)
So:
\(E = \frac{5}{9} + \frac{25}{6} - \frac{10}{9}\)
Combine terms:
\(\frac{5}{9} - \frac{10}{9} = -\frac{5}{9}\)
So:
\(E = \frac{25}{6} - \frac{5}{9}\)
Common denominator \(18\):
\(\frac{25}{6} = \frac{75}{18}, \quad \frac{5}{9} = \frac{10}{18}\)
So:
\(E = \frac{75}{18} - \frac{10}{18} = \frac{65}{18}\)



Final answer
\(\boxed{\frac{65}{18} \approx 3.61}\)

title: Drunk postman
text:
This problem studies the case of a drunk postman who has to deliver \(n\) letter and \(n\) boxes but assigns each letter randomly.

Question 1: Right permutation
What is the probability that each letter goes to the right box ?






Tip💡 Solution





Since \(Card(\mathcal{S}_n) = n!\), we have \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}( \sigma=id)=\frac{1}{n!}}\)





Question 2: At least one letter right
What is the probability that at least one letter goes to the right box ?






Tip💡 Hint





Define the event \(A_i\) : “The letter i goes to the box i” and use the Poincare formula for the probability of the union.









Tip💡 Solution





Define the event \(A_i\) : “The letter i goes to the box i, since a good permutation let’s i unchanged and randomly permutes the others, we get \(\mathbb{P}(A_i) = \frac{(n-1)!}{n!} = \frac{1}{n}\)
By the Poincare formula, we find
\(\mathbb{P}(\bigcup_{i=1}^n A_i) = \sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k-1} \sum_{1\le i_1 < ... < i_k  \le n} \mathbb{P}(A_{i_1} \cap ... \cap A_{i_k})=\sum_{k=1}^n (-1)^{k-1}\binom{n}{k}\frac{(n-k)!}{n!} = \sum_{k=1}^n \frac{(-1)^{k-1}}{k!}.\)
Accordingly, we have \[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one good letter})=1-\sum_{k=0}^n \frac{(-1)^{k}}{k!} \rightarrow_{n\to\infty} 1-e^{-1}\approx0.632.}\]





Question 3: No right letter
What is the probability that no letters are delivered to the right box ?






Tip💡 Solution





We have \[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{no good letter})= 1-\mathbb{P}(\text{at least one good letter})=e^{-1} \approx 0.368.}\]
We can find the number of ways that no letter are right delivered: probability one permutation leeds to no good letter * number of permutations : \(d_n = n!e^{-1}.\)

title: Where are the Aces ?
text:
What is the expected number of cards that we need to draw from a standard card pack before the first ace to appear (including that ace) ?






Tip💡 Hint





For each of the remaining cards, account the different possibilities.









Tip💡 Solution





Let \(N\) be the random variable that counts the number of cards. Therefore, we have \(\mathbb{E}[N] = 1+\sum_{k=1}^{48} \mathbb{P}(\text{card k before first ace}).\)
For each of the 48 remaining cards, we only have 5 possibilities of the order respect to the Aces: 1 A 2 A 3 A 4 A 5. The only possibility that counts for us is the first one. Since all the cards are drawn with the same probability, \(\mathbb{P}(\text{card k before first ace}) = 1/5\).
Thus, \(\mathbb{E}[N] = 1 +\frac{48}{5} = \frac{53}{5}=10.6.\)

title: Lost key in the last classroom
text:
The keeper of a high school lost the key of the school in one of the 123 rooms with a probability \(p\). He already searched the key in 122 rooms and it wasn’t there. What is the probability that the lost key is in the last room ?






Tip💡 Hint





If we were sure that the key was in the high school then it will surely be in the last classroom. But, what happens if we are not sure that the key is even in the school.









Tip💡 Solution





Let’s denote three different events:

A: “The key is in the school” \(\mathbb{P}(A) = p\)
B: “The key is in the last classroom” \(\mathbb{P}(B) = \mathbb{P}(A)*\mathbb{P}(B|A) + \mathbb{P}(\bar{A})*\mathbb{P}(B|\bar{A}) = p*\frac{1}{123}+(1-p)*0 = \frac{p}{123}\)
C: “The key is not found in the first 122 rooms”: \(\mathbb{P}(C) = \mathbb{P}(A)*\mathbb{P}(C|A) + \mathbb{P}(\bar{A})*\mathbb{P}(C|\bar{A}) = p*\frac{1}{123}+(1-p)*1 = 1-p+\frac{p}{123}\)

The problem asks for \(\mathbb{P}(B|C).\)
By Bayes’s theorem, we have \(\mathbb{P}(B|C) = \mathbb{P}(C|B)\frac{\mathbb{P}(B)}{\mathbb{P}(C)}.\)
Accordingly, we get \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(B|C) = 1*\frac{\frac{p}{123}}{1-p+\frac{p}{123}}=\frac{p}{123-122p}.}\)
If we are sure that the keeper lost his key in the school (ie \(p=1\)), then we find that the key is surely in the last classroom \(\mathbb{P}(B|C) = 1.\)

title: Local minima in a permutation
text:
What is the expected number of local minima in a random permutation ?






Tip💡 Hint





How can every integer can be a local minimum in the permutation ?









Tip💡 Solution





Let’s suppose that we have a permutation with \(n\) elements: \(u \in \mathbb{S}_n.\)

For \(k \in {2, ..., n-1}\), k is a local minimum if \(u(k)\le u(k-1)\) and \(u(k)\le u(k+1).\) Since the permutation is random each of the three number could be the smallest one with equiprobability. Thus \(\forall \; 2 \le k \le n-1, \mathbb{P}(k \; \text{local minimum}) = 1/3.\)
For \(k=1\), k is a local minimum if \(u(k)\le u(k+1).\) Thus, \(\mathbb{P}(k \; \text{local minimum}) = 1/2.\)
For \(k=n\), k is a local minimum if \(u(k)\le u(k-1).\) Thus, \(\mathbb{P}(k \; \text{local minimum}) = 1/2.\)

Finally, we have \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[N] = (n-2)* \frac{1}{3} + 2 * \frac{1}{2} = \frac{n+1}{3}.}\]

title: Operation on Uniform distributions
text:
Let’s suppose that we have two fair dices ( \(U_1 \sim \mathcal{U}(\{1,...,6\}), U_2 \sim \mathcal{U}(\{1,...,6\}), U_1 \perp U_2\)). Let \(X = min(U_1, U_2) \; \text{and} \; Y = max(U_1, U_2).\)

\(\mathbb{E}[X]\) ?






Tip💡 Hint





Find \(\mathbb{P}(X=k)\) and compute the expectation









Tip💡 Solution





Let \(1 \le k\le6\), we have \((X=k) = (U_1 = k \; \cap \; U_2 = k) \cup (U_1 = k \; \cap \; U_2 > k) \cup (U_1 > k \; \cap \; U_2 = k).\) Out of the 36 possible outcomes, the first event happens \(6\) times, the second \(6-k\) times and the third also \(6-k\) times. Thus \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X=k) = \frac{1}{36}+ \frac{6-i}{36}+ \frac{6-i}{36}=\frac{13-2i}{36}}.\)
Finally, we compute \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X] = \sum k\mathbb{P}(X=k) = \frac{11}{36}+2*\frac{9}{36}+3*\frac{7}{36}+4*\frac{5}{36}+5*\frac{3}{36}+6*\frac{1}{36} = \frac{91}{36}\approx 2.52}\]





\(\mathbb{E}[Y]\) ?






Tip💡 Hint





We don’t need to do the same as in the first question.









Tip💡 Solution





We have \(X + Y =U_1 + U_2\), thus by linearity of the expectation, \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[U_1] + \mathbb{E}[U_2]-\mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{7}{2} + \frac{7}{2} - \frac{91}{36} = \frac{161}{36}}\]





\(cov(X,Y)\) ?






Tip💡 Hint





Use a similar trick as in the second question.









Tip💡 Solution





We have \(cov(X,Y) = \mathbb{E}[XY] -\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[U_1U_2] -\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y] = \mathbb{E}[U_1]\mathbb{E}[U_2] -\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y].\)
Thus, \[\boxed{cov(X,Y) = \frac{7}{2} \frac{7}{2} - \frac{91}{36} \frac{161}{36} = \frac{1225}{1296}.}\]

title: Muffin supply probability
text:
Question
In a bakery, each customer independently has a \(70\%\) chance of ordering a croissant and a \(30\%\) chance of ordering a muffin.
There are \(2\) muffins left and \(5\) customers.
What is the probability that the muffins are enough?






Tip💡 Solution





Let \(X\) be the number of customers (out of \(5\)) who order muffins.
Then:
\(X \sim \text{Bin}(5, 0.3)\)
We want:
\(P(X \le 2)\)


Step 1: Break into cases
\(P(X \le 2) = P(X=0) + P(X=1) + P(X=2)\)



Step 2: Compute each term

Case 1: \(X=0\)
\(P(X=0) = (0.7)^5 = 0.16807\)



Case 2: \(X=1\)
\(P(X=1) = \binom{5}{1}(0.3)(0.7)^4\)
\(= 5 \cdot 0.3 \cdot 0.2401 = 0.36015\)



Case 3: \(X=2\)
\(P(X=2) = \binom{5}{2}(0.3)^2(0.7)^3\)
\(= 10 \cdot 0.09 \cdot 0.343 = 0.3087\)




Step 3: Add probabilities
\(P(X \le 2) = 0.16807 + 0.36015 + 0.3087\)
\(P(X \le 2) = 0.83692\)



Final answer
\(\boxed{0.83692 \approx 0.837}\)

title: Poisson distribution
text:
Suppose \(X\sim \mathcal{P}(\lambda)\)

Question 1: \(\mathbb{E}[X | X >0]\) ?






Tip💡 Solution





We have \(\mathbb{E}[X | X >0] = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k\mathbb{P}(X=k | X>0) = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} k\frac{\mathbb{P}(X=k \cap X>0)}{\mathbb{P}(X>0)} = \sum_{k=1}^{+\infty} k \frac{\lambda^k e^{-\lambda}}{k!(1-e^{-\lambda})} = \frac{e^{-\lambda}}{1-e^{-\lambda}}\sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^{k+1}}{k!} = \frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}.\) Thus \[\boxed{\mathbb{E}[X | X >0] = \frac{\lambda}{1-e^{-\lambda}}.}\]





Question 2: \(\mathbb{P}(X \in 2\mathbb{N})\)






Tip💡 Solution





We have \(\mathbb{P}(X \in 2\mathbb{N}) = \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{\lambda^{2k} e^{-\lambda}}{(2k)!}.\) From the power series expansions, we know \(e^x =  \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!},\) thus \(e^x + e^{-x} =  \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{x^k}{k!} +  \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} (-1)^k \frac{x^k}{k!} =2 \sum_{k=0}^{+\infty} \frac{x^{2k}}{(2k)!}.\) Therefore, \[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(X \in 2\mathbb{N}) = e^{-\lambda}\frac{e^{-\lambda} + e^{\lambda}}{2}=\frac{1+e^{-2\lambda}}{2}.}\]

title: Polya’s urn
text:
An urn initially contains b white balls and r red balls. The following experiment is carried out: * A ball is drawn from the urn at random, and its color is noted. * The ball is returned to the urn, and d balls of the same color are added. The experiment is repeated as many times as desired. Let \(n \ge 1\). Determine the probability that the ball drawn will be white on the nth draw.






Tip💡 Hint





Compute the probability for the first draw, the second, the third. Then make a guess for the general formula and prove it by induction.









Tip💡 Solution





We denote by \(W_n\) the event the a white ball is drew from the nth draw. Let \(P_n : \mathbb{P}(W_n)=\frac{b}{b+r}\)

Initialisation : for \(n=1\), there are \(b\) white balls among the \(b+r\) total balls so the formula is correct at the step 1
Heredity: Let \(n \ge 1\). Assume that the result is true for \(n \ge 1\).We cannot use \(\mathbb{P}(W_{n+1}  | W_n)\) in our calculations, because we do not know exactly how many balls are in the urn when \(W_n\) is true. Except for \(W_1\). After one draw, if \(W_1\) is true, we have $ b + d $ white balls and $ r$ red balls. To reach \(n + 1\) draws, there remain \(n\) draws to perform. This is exactly equivalent to performing \(n\) draws starting with \(b_0 = b + d\) white balls and \(r_0 = r\) red balls. Thus, by the induction hypothesis, we deduce: \(\mathbb{P}(W_{n+1} | W_1) = \frac{b_0}{b_0 + r_0} = \frac{b + d}{b + d + r}\). Likewise, in the other case, we have \(\mathbb{P}(W_{n+1} | \bar{W_1}) = \frac{b}{b + d + r}.\) Accordingly, \(\mathbb{P}(W_{n+1}) = \mathbb{P}(W_{n+1} \mid W_1)\mathbb{P}(W_1) + \mathbb{P}(W_{n+1} \mid \bar{W_1})\mathbb{P}(\bar{W_1})] = \frac{b + d}{b + d + r} \times \frac{b}{b + r} + \frac{b}{b + d + r} \times \frac{r}{b + r}.\) Finally, \(\mathbb{P}(W_{n+1})=\frac{b}{b+r}\)

By the principle of the induction proof, \(\boxed{\forall n \in \mathbb{N}^*, \mathbb{P}(W_n)=\frac{b}{b+r}}\)

title: Stopping time for HH or TT
text:
Question
We flip a fair coin until we obtain either HH or TT for the first time. What is the probability that the total number of flips is even?






Tip💡 Solution





We stop the first time we see two consecutive identical outcomes (HH or TT).
Let \(T\) be the stopping time.


Step 1: Understanding the process
After the first flip, each new flip behaves as follows:

with probability \(1/2\), it matches the previous flip → the process stops
with probability \(1/2\), it differs → the process continues

So at each step after the first, we either stop or continue, each with probability \(1/2\).



Step 2: Probability of stopping at a given time
To stop at time \(2k\), we must:

survive \(2k-2\) steps (always alternating)
then stop at step \(2k\)

Each step of survival has probability \(1/2\), and stopping also has probability \(1/2\).
So:

to reach time \(2\): probability \(1/2\)
to reach time \(4\): probability \((1/2)^3\)
to reach time \(6\): probability \((1/2)^5\)

In general:
\(\mathbb{P}(T = 2k) = (1/2)^{2k-1}\)



Step 3: Sum over even stopping times
We compute:
\(\mathbb{P}(T \text{ is even}) = \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1/2)^{2k-1}\)
Factor out \(1/2\):
\(= (1/2)\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} (1/4)^{k-1}\)
This is a geometric series:
\(\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^k = \frac{1}{1-r}\)
So:
\(= (1/2)\cdot \frac{1}{1-1/4}\)
\(= (1/2)\cdot \frac{4}{3}\)
\(= \frac{2}{3}\)



Final answer
\(\boxed{\frac{2}{3}}\)

title: Tournament between two divisions
text:
Suppose we have n teams in the division 1 and n teams in the division 2 and we create a a tournament across those teams (only 1 match).

Question 1: Different division for all
What is the probability that each in each match all teams compete against a team from the other division (let’s denote the probability by \(a_n\)). Also, give a equivalent as \(n \to + \infty\) using Stirling formula: \(n! \sim_{+\infty} \sqrt{2\pi n} (\frac{n}{e})^n.\)






Tip💡 Hint





Try to associate sequentially each team from division 1 to a team from division 2









Tip💡 Solution






In order to create matches in different divisions, for the first team in the division 1 we have n choices then, for the second team in division 1 we only have n-1 choices.
The total number of possible matches is created by associated to the first team in division 1 any of the other 2n-1 teams. Then, for the second team in division 1 (suppose it was not the one chosen), we have to assign one of the 2n-3 teams remaining (the total number of teams - the two from the first match - itself).

Thus, we have \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(a_n)=\frac{n(n-1)...1}{(2n-1)(2n-3)...1}= \frac{n!}{\frac{(2n)!}{(2n)(2n-2)...2}} = \frac{2^n(n!)^2}{(2n)!}.}\)
For the equivalent in \(+\infty\), we get from the Stirling’s formula \(\mathbb{P}(a_n) \sim_{+\infty} \frac{2^n * (\sqrt{2\pi n} (\frac{n}{e})^n)^2}{\sqrt{2\pi 2n} (\frac{2n}{e})^{2n}}= \frac{\frac{n^{2n}}{e^{2n}}}{\frac{n^{2n}}{e^{2n}}}\times \frac{2^n}{2^{2n}} \times \frac{2\pi n}{2\sqrt{\pi n}} = \frac{\sqrt{\pi n}}{2^n}.\)





Question 2: Same division for all
What is the probability that each in each match all teams compete against a team from the same division (let’s denote the probability by \(b_n\)). Also, give a equivalent as \(n \to + \infty\) using Stirling formula: \(n! \sim_{+\infty} \sqrt{2\pi n} (\frac{n}{e})^n.\)






Tip💡 Hint





Since, we can create matches for all teams in the same division, that means that \(n \in 2\mathbb{N}\). Try to associate sequentially each team to a team from the same division.









Tip💡 Solution





Since, we can create matches for all teams in the same division, that means that n is even so we will have that we have 2n teams in division 1 and 2n teams in division 2.

In order to create matches in same division, for the first team in the division 1 we have 2n-1 choices then, for the third team in division 1 we only have 2n-3 choices. But the same happens in the division 2.
The total number of possible matches is created by associated to the first team in division 1 any of the other 4n-1 teams. Then, for the second team in division 1 (suppose it was not the one chosen), we have to assign one of the 4n-3 teams remaining (the total number of teams - the two from the first match - itself).

Thus, we have \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(b_{2n})=\frac{(2n-1)(2n-3)...1 * (2n-1)(2n-3)...1}{(4n-1)(4n-3)...1}= \frac{\frac{(2n)!}{2^n n!}\times \frac{(2n)!}{2^nn!}}{\frac{(4n)!}{2^{2n}(2n)!}} = \frac{(2n)!^3}{(4n)!n!^2}.}\)
For the equivalent in \(+\infty\), we get from the Stirling’s formula \(\mathbb{P}(b_{2n}) \sim_{+\infty} \frac{(\sqrt{2\pi 2n} (\frac{2n}{e})^{2n})^3}{\sqrt{2\pi 4n} (\frac{4n}{e})^{4n} \times(\sqrt{2\pi n} (\frac{n}{e})^n)^2}= \frac{(\frac{n}{e})^{6n}}{(\frac{n}{e})^{6n}} \times \frac{2^{6n}}{2^{8n}} \times \frac{8(\pi n)^{3/2}}{2(2 \pi n)^{1/2}*2 \pi n}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}*2^{2n}} = \sqrt{2} * 2^{-2n}\)

title: Uniform Ratio
text:
Let \(X\sim \mathbb{U}([0,1]), Y\sim \mathbb{U}([0,1]), X \perp Y\), what is \(\mathbb{P}(1 \le X/Y \le2)\) ?






Tip💡 Hint





Compute the partial area corresponding to the meeting.









Tip💡 Solution





Since the two uniforms are positive, the possible region is \[\begin{cases} 0 \le x \le 1 \\ 0\le y \le 1\end{cases}.\]
The condition if fulfilled if
\[\begin{cases} x / y\le 2\\  x/y \ge 1  \end{cases} \sim \begin{cases} y \le x \\  y \le x/2  \end{cases}.\]
We can plot the regions and we find \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(1 \le X/Y \le2) = \frac{1-\frac{1*1}{2}-\frac{1*1/2}{2}}{1}= 1/4.}\)


















Tip🚨 Generalisation





What if we wanted a ratio between p and q ?
Thus, \[\boxed{\mathbb{P}(p \le X/Y \le q) = 1-\frac{1*p}{2} -\frac{1*1/q}{2} = 1-\frac{p+1/q}{2}.}\]

title: Separation of the balls into urns
text:
Suppose we have r balls indiscernible and n urns (\(r \le n\)).
What is the probability that each urn has at most one ball ?






Tip💡 Hint





Try to compute the number of different sequences of ball / urn separation that we can do.









Tip💡 Solution





Let’s denote by * the balls and by | the separation of the different urns. Therefore, one possibility to dispach the balls is the following "*|*|...|*". Accordingly, we need to choose the right place for the separators within the sequence.

The total number of sequence that we can do is \(\binom{n+r-1}{n-1}\) (we choose the place of the separators)
The total number of sequence verifying that all urns have at most one ball is \(\binom {n}{r}\) (we choose the urns that have exactly one ball).

Thus \(\boxed{\mathbb{P}(\text{All urns have at most one ball}) = \frac{\binom {n}{r}}{\binom{n+r-1}{n-1}}= \frac{(n-1)...(n-r+1)}{(n+r-1)...(n+1)}.}\)









Tip🚨 Follow up





The probability that there exist one urn with at least two balls is thus \(1-\mathbb{P}(\text{All urns have at most one ball}).\)
Moreover, if the balls were discernible, for each ball we could choose an urn with no ball yet. We will get a different probability : \(\mathbb{P}(\text{All urns have at most one ball})=\frac{n(n-1)...(n-r+1)}{n^r}.\)

title: Pricing options with Black-Sholes-Merton and Monte Carlo in C++
PCA on the Pokemon stats
text:
In this project, I apply a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) to the six battle statistics of Pokemon — HP, Attack, Defense, Special Attack, Special Defense and Speed — and explore how the full Pokédex sits in the resulting 2D spaces. The analysis covers all six generations of the CSV (~721 species), with a specific pass on the subset of final evolutions and a final view with legendaries highlighted against the rest.
Going from 6 dimensions to 2 is a modest reduction, so this project is really about exploring structure rather than dramatic compression. The interpretation comes from reading the loadings of each principal component and pairing the scatter with a biplot.

The dataset
The stats come from the well-known Pokemon with stats dataset originally published on Kaggle by Alberto Barradas and mirrored as a stable raw CSV on GitHub Gist. The CSV covers Generations 1 through 6, one row per species (plus Mega / Primal forme rows which we drop upstream). Download it directly here: pokemon.csv. To restrict the analysis to one or a few generations, pass generations=[1] (or any iterable) to load_pokemon.
The CSV does not flag final evolutions, so I hand-curated the complement: a NON_FINALS set of every species that has a further evolution within Gen 1-6. Any Pokemon not in that set is treated as a final evolution. Cross-generational evolutions demote the earlier forms (Onix is non-final because of Steelix, Magneton because of Magnezone, and so on).


The PCA pipeline
The six stats share a nominal 1-255 scale but their empirical variances differ, so each stat is standardized (zero mean, unit variance) before the PCA is fit. The interpretation of the first three components (even though we only keep two) is:

PC1 — sum of loadings is positive, so higher PC1 means more overall power.
PC2 — HP + Sp. Def loading sums negative, so lower PC2 means bulkier / more defensive.
PC3 — Attack loading is positive, so higher PC3 means leans physical (vs special).

The signs do not affect any distance or variance, only how the chart reads.
On the ~721 Pokemon in the CSV, the first two components typically capture around 62% of the total variance, with PC1 dominated by offensive and defensive stats together (the “size of the Pokemon”), PC2 contrasting bulk against speed. If we add the third we get 73% of total variance and PC3 is picking up physical-vs-special.


Baseline view: every Pokemon, Total-coloured
A first plain scatter of all ~721 Pokemon on PC1-PC2. Points are coloured by their Total stat as a sanity check — since PC1 is the overall-power axis, the colour gradient should line up neatly along PC1.


Coloured by primary type
Same points, now coloured by the Pokemon’s primary type (Type 1). Dual-type Pokemon are still shown under their primary type only — the secondary type appears on hover. I am using brightened versions of the canonical type colours so everything reads well on dark.
Honest expectation: types are gameplay categories, not stat-determining labels, so heavy overlap is normal. The chart is useful for spotting which types skew along PC1 or PC2 (e.g. Steel and Rock sit high on defensive stats; Flying leans offensive-fast) rather than for finding clean clusters.


Final evolutions only
Next I restrict to every final evolution across Gen 1-6 and re-fit the PCA on that subset. This matters: the principal axes depend on the covariance of the data they are fit on. If I only projected final evolutions using the axes learned from the full population, I would still be looking at directions that separate weak from strong Pokemon. Re-fitting means the axes now capture the variance among final evolutions, which is the more interesting question here.


Legendaries highlighted
Finally, the full population again — non-legendaries drawn dim so they act as context, legendaries in the accent colour, enlarged and labeled. PC1 tracks total stats by construction, so legendaries cluster on the high-PC1 side (that is the sanity check, not the finding). The interesting structure is PC2 and PC3: the Articuno-Zapdos-Moltres triad should split along the bulk-vs-speed axis, while Mewtwo sits out in pure offensive power, and creatures like Lugia or Ho-Oh trade offense for extreme bulk.


Trying it yourself
To run the full pipeline in one place, I aggregated every .py into a single Jupyter notebook. Download it here: pokemon_pca_notebook.ipynb. The only requirements are pandas, scikit-learn and plotly.

  var_vec[2]  <- val2 
  # Calculer les valeurs pour h = 2 à horizon
  for (h in 2:horizon) {
    var_vec[h+1] <- (1 / (1 - phi)) * (val2 - phi * val1 + (val1 - val2) * phi^h) #t_X_t+h
  } 
  # Retourner le vecteur complet
  return(var_vec)
}
#Calculer la variance des écarts
variance <- function(phi, theta, sigma2, horizon) {
  # Initialise vecteur résultats
  var_vec <- numeric(horizon + 1)
  var_vec[1] <- 0  # pour h=0
  
  for (h in 1:horizon) {
    sum_k <- 0
    for (k in 0:(h-1)) {
      val_k <- (1 - phi^(k+1) + theta + theta * phi^k) / (1 - phi)
      sum_k <- sum_k + val_k^2
    }
    var_vec[h+1] <- sigma2 * sum_k
  }
  
  return(var_vec)
}
